issues.legal_issue: A grandson does not acquire a birth-based coparcenary interest in property that devolves upon his father under the statutory rules of intestate succession before the grandson is born.
material_facts: The property had been joint family property, but its owner died before the grandson was born, leaving a son and three daughters.
The son and daughters inherited equal shares, and the shares were recorded and partitioned among them.
The grandson was born after that succession had opened, while his father was alive.
issues.conclusion: The grandson acquired no interest in the property by birth; the property inherited by his father did not remain joint family property with the grandson.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 displace inconsistent pre-existing Hindu law and provide for intestate succession to a male's property; a grandson whose father is alive is not a Class I heir in that succession. Under Section 19, heirs succeed per capita as tenants in common, not per stirpes as joint tenants. Section 6 did not apply to these facts. The Court applied Commissioner of Wealth Tax v. Chander Sen, (1986) 3 SCR 254, and its reaffirmation in Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar, (1987) 1 SCR 516, Sunderdas Thackersay & Bros. v. Commissioner of Income-tax, 1982 (137) ITR 646, Commissioner of Income Tax v. P.L. Karuppan Chettiar, 1993 Supp. (1) SCC 580, and Additional Commissioner of Income-tax v. M. Karthikeyan, 1994 Supp. (2) SCC 112. Sheela Devi v. Lal Chand, (2006) 8 SCC 581, was distinguished because it concerned property governed by coparcenary succession.

rule.if: civil_appeal_about_inherited_property and deceased_died_intestate and property_devolved_to_father_and_daughters and heirs_took_per_capita_as_tenants_in_common and grandfather_died_before_grandson_was_born and father_was_alive

predicates.civil_appeal_about_inherited_property: A civil appeal concerns a claim to an interest in property inherited from a deceased person.
predicates.deceased_died_intestate: The property owner died without a will governing the property's devolution.
predicates.property_devolved_to_father_and_daughter: The deceased owner's son and daughters inherited the property.
predicates.heirs_took_per_capita_as_tenants_in_comm: The heirs received individual shares in their own right rather than inheriting jointly by family branches.
predicates.grandfather_died_before_grandson_was_bor: The owner died before the claimant grandson was born.
predicates.father_was_alive: The claimant's father was alive when the succession to the property took place.

issues.definition: When an intestate owner's property passes in individual shares to the owner's son and daughters before a grandson is born, and the grandson's father is alive, the grandson has no birth-based coparcenary interest in that property.

issues.legal_issue: A father who inherits an individual share and receives property allotted to him on partition may transfer that property without proving legal necessity.
material_facts: The deceased owner's son and daughters inherited equal shares and partitioned the properties among themselves.
The properties allotted to the father were treated as his individual share, and he mortgaged and later sold the disputed land.
The grandson challenged the transfers on the ground that they were not supported by legal necessity.
issues.conclusion: The father was entitled to transfer the land falling within his allotted share, and the transfers could not be set aside for want of proof of legal necessity.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 8 and 19 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 make heirs to such property individual tenants in common, taking per capita rather than per stirpes. Since the property allotted to the father was his individual share and Section 6 did not apply, the restrictions on a coparcenary manager's alienation for legal necessity did not govern his transfer. The Court relied on the principles in Commissioner of Wealth Tax v. Chander Sen, (1986) 3 SCR 254, and the related authorities reaffirming it, including Yudhishter v. Ashok Kumar, (1987) 1 SCR 516.

rule.if: civil_appeal_challenging_property_transfer and heirs_inherited_individual_shares and heirs_partitioned_the_property and father_transferred_only_property_allotted_to_him and transfer_challenged_for_lack_of_necessity

predicates.civil_appeal_challenging_property_transf: A civil appeal challenges a transfer of inherited property.
predicates.heirs_inherited_individual_shares: The heirs inherited distinct individual shares in the property.
predicates.heirs_partitioned_the_property: The heirs divided the property among themselves and received separate allotments.
predicates.father_transferred_only_property_allotte: The father transferred property that had been allotted to his own share.
predicates.transfer_challenged_for_lack_of_necessit: A claimant challenged the transfer on the ground that it was not made for legal necessity.

issues.definition: When heirs take individual shares and partition the property, a father may transfer property allotted to his share without proving legal necessity, even if the transfer is challenged on that ground.
